steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a machine translation paper proposing to distill the quality gains of MBR decoding and QE reranking into the model at training time by finetuning, so that cheap decoding can be used at inference. Motivate it and end with a contributions list.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Common decoding methods and the case for MBR decoding
- Drawback: cost of MBR decoding
- Proposal: distill gains at training time; QE reranking as cheaper alternative
- This work: finetuning NMT models on MBR/QE outputs
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Decoding methods
  - beam search, greedy: most common for NLG incl. NMT
  - prior work (cite): MAP decoding (approximates most likely prediction from model probabilities) suboptimal for NMT, misaligned probability distributions
  - proposed MBR decoding instead: not highest model probability, but highest estimated quality w.r.t. utility metric
  - follow-up (cite): MBR with neural utility metrics BLEURT (cite), COMET (cite) significantly beats beam search, expert-based human evaluation
- Cost
  - prohibitively expensive
  - large number n of candidates per input query, (expensive) scoring on every pair (n_{i},n_{j}) -> O(n^{2})
- Proposal
  - distill MBR quality gains at training time, no effect on decoding speed / resource usage
  - MBR still slow even for generating distillation data
  - alternative: rerank same candidates with neural quality estimation (QE) metric; linear not quadratic
  - prior work (cite): reranking with neural metrics better than beam search, similar benefits to MBR
- This work
  - NMT; finetune on MBR-decoded and QE-reranked outputs from monolingual sources
  - self-training or external teacher; efficient decoding (beam search) at inference
- Contributions
  - MBR finetuning and QE finetuning
  - significantly beat base model, two language pairs; beam search output finetuning degrades quality
  - additional gains on top of model finetuned on human translations
  - LLM teacher substantially better than self-teacher
  - LLM teacher from base student even beats finetuning on human translations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The most common decoding methods used for Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, and also for neural machine translation (NMT), are beam search and greedy decoding. But earlier work showed that maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding methods are suboptimal for NMT, because the probability distributions are misaligned. MAP methods approximate the most likely prediction based on the model probabilities. That work proposed Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding instead as an alternative decoding method. MBR decoding, unlike MAP decoding, does not try to produce the prediction (i.e. translation) with the highest estimated model probability. It chooses the prediction that is estimated to have the highest quality with respect to a utility metric. A follow-up study showed that MBR decoding with neural utility metrics like BLEURT and COMET significantly outperforms beam search decoding, according to expert-based human evaluation.

The main drawback of MBR decoding is that it is prohibitively expensive. The algorithm requires that for every input query a large number n of candidates are generated from the model, and then an (expensive) scoring function has to be computed on every pair of distinct candidates (n_{i},n_{j}), so O(n^{2}) computations in total.

MBR decoding gives significant quality improvements relative to beam search, so we propose to distill the MBR quality gains at training time, without affecting decoding speed or resource usage. But the slow inference speed of MBR decoding is still a limitation even when generating the distillation data. As an alternative we can rerank the same candidate model predictions with a neural quality estimation (QE) metric. Reranking is faster than MBR decoding because its inference cost scales linearly with the number of candidate predictions and not quadratically. Other work showed that reranking with neural metrics produces better predictions than beam search, and has similar benefits to MBR decoding.

- This work: NMT; finetune on MBR-decoded / QE-reranked outputs from monolingual sources; self-training or external teacher; beam search at inference
- Contributions
  - MBR finetuning, QE finetuning
  - beat base model on two language pairs; beam search finetuning degrades
  - gains on top of human-translation finetuned model
  - LLM teacher > self-teacher
  - LLM teacher even beats finetuning on human translations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The most common decoding methods used for Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, and also for neural machine translation (NMT), are beam search and greedy decoding. But earlier work showed that maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding methods are suboptimal for NMT, because the probability distributions are misaligned. MAP methods approximate the most likely prediction based on the model probabilities. That work proposed Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding instead as an alternative decoding method. MBR decoding, unlike MAP decoding, does not try to produce the prediction (i.e. translation) with the highest estimated model probability. It chooses the prediction that is estimated to have the highest quality with respect to a utility metric. A follow-up study showed that MBR decoding with neural utility metrics like BLEURT and COMET significantly outperforms beam search decoding, according to expert-based human evaluation.

The main drawback of MBR decoding is that it is prohibitively expensive. The algorithm requires that for every input query a large number n of candidates are generated from the model, and then an (expensive) scoring function has to be computed on every pair of distinct candidates (n_{i},n_{j}), so O(n^{2}) computations in total.

MBR decoding gives significant quality improvements relative to beam search, so we propose to distill the MBR quality gains at training time, without affecting decoding speed or resource usage. But the slow inference speed of MBR decoding is still a limitation even when generating the distillation data. As an alternative we can rerank the same candidate model predictions with a neural quality estimation (QE) metric. Reranking is faster than MBR decoding because its inference cost scales linearly with the number of candidate predictions and not quadratically. Other work showed that reranking with neural metrics produces better predictions than beam search, and has similar benefits to MBR decoding.

In this work we focus on the NMT task. We show that we can get the quality gains of MBR decoding and QE reranking by finetuning NMT models on MBR-decoded and QE-reranked outputs generated from monolingual sources, either with self-training or with an external teacher model, and then using a more efficient decoding method (such as beam search) at inference time.

Our contributions are:

- • We propose two finetuning methods, MBR finetuning and QE finetuning. They distill the performance gains from MBR decoding and QE reranking respectively at training time, and avoid expensive decoding at inference time.

- • On the NMT task we show that these finetuning methods significantly outperform the base model across two language pairs, while finetuning on beam search output makes quality worse.

- • We show that MBR and QE finetuning on top of a model finetuned on human translations both give additional quality improvements.

- • We show that using a LLM as the teacher model is substantially better than using a self-teacher for MBR and QE finetuning.

- • Also, MBR and QE finetuning from the base student model with a LLM teacher even outperforms finetuning on human translations.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Beam search and greedy decoding are the most common decoding methods for Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, including neural machine translation (NMT). However, [1] showed that maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding methods, which approximate the most likely prediction based on model probabilities, are suboptimal for NMT because of misaligned probability distributions. They proposed Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding as an alternative decoding method. Unlike MAP decoding, MBR decoding does not aim to produce the prediction (i.e. translation) with the highest estimated model probability; instead, it chooses the prediction estimated to have the highest quality with respect to a utility metric. A follow-up study by [2] showed that MBR decoding with neural utility metrics like BLEURT [3] and COMET [4] significantly outperforms beam search decoding according to expert-based human evaluation.

However, the main drawback of MBR decoding is that it is prohibitively expensive. The algorithm requires that, for every input query, a large number n of candidates be generated from the model, and that an (expensive) scoring function then be computed on every pair of distinct candidates (n_{i},n_{j}), for a total of O(n^{2}) computations.

Given the significant quality improvements of MBR decoding over beam search, we propose to distill the MBR quality gains at training time, without affecting decoding speed or resource usage. Even so, the slow inference speed of MBR decoding remains a limitation when generating distillation data. As an alternative, we can rerank the same candidate model predictions using a neural quality estimation (QE) metric. Reranking is faster than MBR decoding, because its inference cost scales linearly rather than quadratically with the number of candidate predictions. [5] showed that reranking with neural metrics produces better predictions than beam search and has similar benefits to MBR decoding.

In this work, we focus on the task of NMT and show that we can benefit from the quality gains of MBR decoding and QE reranking by finetuning NMT models on MBR-decoded and QE-reranked outputs generated from monolingual sources, either via self-training or using an external teacher model, and then using a more efficient decoding method (such as beam search) at inference time.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We propose two finetuning methods, MBR finetuning and QE finetuning, which distill the performance gains of MBR decoding and QE reranking, respectively, at training time while avoiding expensive decoding at inference time.

- • Using the task of NMT, we show that these finetuning methods significantly outperform the base model across two language pairs, whereas finetuning on beam search output degrades quality.

- • We show that both MBR and QE finetuning on top of a model finetuned on human translations yield additional quality improvements.

- • We show that using a LLM as the teacher model substantially outperforms using a self-teacher for MBR and QE finetuning.

- • Moreover, both MBR and QE finetuning from the base student model using a LLM teacher even outperform finetuning on human translations.

References:
[1] Eikema & Aziz (2020) Bryan Eikema and Wilker Aziz. Is map decoding all you need? the inadequacy of the mode in neural machine translation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.10283 , 2020.
[2] Freitag et al. (2022a) Markus Freitag, David Grangier, Qijun Tan, and Bowen Liang. High quality rather than high model probability: Minimum bayes risk decoding with neural metrics. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics , 10:811–825, 2022a.
[3] Sellam et al. (2020) Thibault Sellam, Dipanjan Das, and Ankur P Parikh. Bleurt: Learning robust metrics for text generation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2004.04696 , 2020.
[4] Rei et al. (2020) Ricardo Rei, Craig Stewart, Catarina Farinha, and Alon Lavie. Unbabel’s participation in the wmt20 metrics shared task. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.15535 , 2020.
[5] Fernandes et al. (2022) Patrick Fernandes, António Farinhas, Ricardo Rei, José GC de Souza, Perez Ogayo, Graham Neubig, and André FT Martins. Quality-aware decoding for neural machine translation. arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.00978 , 2022.
